title: A batch no longer means the whole queue
dek: A validated batch limit caps the jobs in each send while leaving the remainder queued for later drains.

sections.title: Each tick took everything waiting
sections.content:
The worker already had a simple path from queued jobs to a send. Its tick function drained the pending array, passed the returned jobs to send at the configured /jobs endpoint, and awaited that call.

The queue helper defined what a batch meant. Calling pending.splice(0) removed every pending job and returned them together. The worker therefore made one send per tick, but the number of jobs in that send depended entirely on the queue length. The shown configuration supplied an endpoint, with no setting for batch size.

sections.title: One send could absorb the entire backlog
sections.content:
A queue of 250 jobs meant a single send containing all 250. There was no way to ask the existing drain helper for only the first 100. PR #108 introduces that boundary: with the default limit, the same queue yields 100 jobs for the current send and keeps 150 for later drains.

The intended guarantee concerns job count. It does not bound the memory occupied by jobs or the time needed to process them. You can control how many jobs enter one send without treating that number as a memory or duration budget.

sections.title: Set the bound where jobs leave the queue
sections.content:
The change connects a validated configuration value to the queue operation. In config.ts, the new batchLimit reads the BATCH_LIMIT environment variable and defaults to 100 when it is absent.

{{CODE:0}}

Validation checks the converted number when the configuration module loads. A fractional value, zero, a negative number, or a value that converts to NaN fails with an explicit error. The worker receives a positive integer rather than silently falling back from an invalid setting.

The central change is in queue.ts. Its drain helper now accepts the bound as a second argument.

{{CODE:1}}

The second argument to splice limits how many jobs the helper removes from the front of the array. The returned batch retains queue order, and jobs beyond the limit stay in the same pending array. If fewer jobs are waiting, the drain returns only those available.

In worker.ts, the tick passes the configured value to that helper before sending the batch.

{{CODE:2}}

Each tick still performs one awaited send. It does not loop until the queue is empty; later drains handle the remainder. Together, the three modified files carry the setting from startup validation to bounded removal and then to the outgoing send.

Per-tenant scheduling remains outside this change because the queue has no tenant key. The batch limit controls the number of jobs selected from the shared queue; it does not introduce tenant-aware selection.

sections.title: Send a bounded batch; retain the rest
sections.content: PR #108 replaces whole-queue drains with a configurable job-count limit, defaulting to 100. Configuration rejects values that are not positive integers at startup, and the worker supplies the validated limit on every tick. Each send receives at most that many jobs while the rest remain queued for later drains. The guarantee stops at batch size: memory use, processing time, and tenant-aware scheduling remain outside it.
